supplement.where: Appendix tables and figures on pp. 13-23 of this PDF; study materials at https://github.com/mismayil/creative-story-gen (p. 9, footnote 2)
supplement.holds: Model list (Tables 6-7, pp. 14-15), story counts per item set (Table 10, p. 23), results stratified by semantic distance (Figures 11, 13, 14) and pronoun/POS/complexity figures. No standard errors or test statistics for the automated-metric comparisons appear in the appendix.

paper_design_summary: Sixty Prolific participants (59 after exclusions) and 60 different LLMs each wrote a five-sentence creative story for four three-word cue sets, giving 431 stories after length filtering. Human and AI stories were compared on automated metrics (n-gram and semantic diversity, novelty, surprise, linguistic complexity) and on creativity ratings by two expert raters, 96 non-expert Prolific raters (on 273 stories), and three LLM judges. No person wrote with AI help.

studies.label: Cue-word short stories by 60 people and 60 LLMs

assignment.what_was_assigned: No people were assigned to AI assistance. Human writers and models independently received the same story prompt.
assignment.quote: Both humans and models were given the same instructions in English using the following prompt:
assignment.locator: p. 3, Methods, Story Generation Data Collection; separate human and model generation procedures
assignment.prereg_locator: Not stated in the full document, including appendices (pp. 1-23).

participants.exclusions: 60 human participants recruited; participants not adhering to instructions were removed, leaving 59. Stories with fewer than 3 or more than 7 sentences were dropped: 480 stories collected (60 humans and 60 models x 4 item sets), 431 kept (208 human, 223 AI; Table 10, p. 23).
participants.who: Prolific participants: fluent English speakers residing in the UK, no language-related disorders, completed secondary school; 43% female, mean age 38.8. Comparison corpus: stories from 60 LLMs (Tables 6-7).
participants.quote: Participants not adhering to instructions were removed, resulting in a total of 59 participants.
participants.locator: p. 3, Methods, Story Generation Data Collection

ai_tool.name_model: 60 LLMs, e.g., GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 405B, Mistral Large (Tables 6-7, pp. 14-15)
ai_tool.how_used: Each model wrote stories zero-shot from the same prompt as the humans (temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95). AI output is compared with human output; no person used AI.

task.description: Write a creative short story of at most five sentences that contains three cue words, avoiding a stated boring storyline; four item sets (stamp-letter-send, petrol-diesel-pump low semantic distance; gloom-payment-exist, organ-empire-comply high).

outcomes.name: Creativity rated by two expert judges (graduate psychology students with creative writing experience; mean of two raters, 5-point scale)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained research assistants, graduate psychology students with creative writing experience, rated all 431 stories. They were blinded to creator identity and their ratings were averaged for each story (p. 5, Human Expert Judges).

contrasts.reported: Table 2, Expert Judges, creativity: Human 3.58 (±0.78) vs AI 2.33 (±0.55); parentheses report SDs. Human n = 208 stories; AI n = 223 stories (p. 23, Table 10). Printed expert-rated advantage for human stories: 1.25 points on a scale of 5; t = −19.34, p < .001.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 2; p. 5, Story Evaluation by Judges; p. 23, Table 10; p. 7, Who's more creative according to our judges?

outcomes.name: Creativity rated by non-expert judges (96 Prolific raters, 5 ratings per story, median rating)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: An independent sample of 96 Prolific judges supplied five ratings per story for a subset of 273 stories. The paper calls the aggregation a median, while parenthetically describing the most common rating; that wording is retained without reinterpretation (p. 5, Human Non-expert Judges). The human/AI story counts within this subset are not stated.

contrasts.reported: Table 2, Non-expert Judges, creativity: Human 2.45 (±0.77) vs AI 3.65 (±0.78); parentheses report SDs. The subset contains 273 stories; creator-specific story counts are not stated. Printed non-expert-rated advantage for AI stories: 1.19 points; t = 12.76, p < .001.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 2; p. 5, Story Evaluation by Judges; p. 7, Who's more creative according to our judges?

outcomes.name: Creativity rated by LLM judges (mean of Claude, Gemini and GPT-4)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Claude, Gemini and GPT-4 each rated all 431 stories; the three model ratings were averaged for creativity, originality, surprise and effectiveness (p. 5, LLM Judges).

contrasts.reported: Table 2, LLM Judges, creativity: Human 2.41 (±0.70) vs AI 4.26 (±0.64); parentheses report SDs. Human n = 208 stories; AI n = 223 stories (p. 23, Table 10). Printed LLM-rated advantage for AI stories: 1.85 points; t = 28.75, p < .001.

outcomes.name: Semantic diversity (inverse homogenization)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean pairwise semantic distance of each story to other stories on the same item set, using gte-large story embeddings and 1 − cosine similarity (p. 4, Diversity). The low/high cue-word semantic-distance stratification is a variant of this outcome (p. 6, Diversity; p. 22, Figure 13b). Lexical n-gram diversity is recorded separately as S1-O7.

contrasts.reported: "We see that humans consistently display a higher lexical and semantic diversity (p < 0.0001)." Figure 2b shows inverse homogenization by item set (figure only, no arm means printed).

diversity_detail.metric: Inverse homogenization: mean pairwise semantic distance, using 1 − cosine similarity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each story against all other stories written on the same item set, excluding itself (p. 4, Diversity). The definition does not explicitly restrict the reference set to stories from the same creator group.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: The method used to obtain the automated-metric p-value is not stated (p. 5, Diversity). No bootstrap, permutation, or independent-pair test is specified.
diversity_detail.notes: This is a comparison of model-generated and unassisted human-generated output. Higher inverse homogenization means greater semantic diversity. Figure 2b is on p. 3; numerical group means and standard errors are not printed.

outcomes.name: Lexical n-gram diversity
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Methods define the ratio of unique n-grams to total n-grams in a story for n = 1 to 5 (p. 4, Diversity); the regression also uses mean n-gram diversity of a story (p. 7). Coded other because this definition is lexical variety within an output rather than semantic diversity across different writers. Figure 2a labels its axis metric_corpus_n_gram_diversity, so the exact corpus aggregation used for that plot is unclear. Figure 13a averages across n-gram sizes and stratifies by cue-word distance (p. 6; p. 22).

contrasts.reported: Humans display higher lexical and semantic diversity (p < 0.0001), reported jointly in the text. Lexical n-gram diversity is plotted in Figure 2a; numerical group levels are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Results, Diversity; p. 3, Figure 2a; p. 4, Diversity

outcomes.name: Thematic diversity (number of theme clusters)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Agglomerative clustering of story embeddings using Ward variance minimization with a threshold of 0.6; theme counts are plotted for human and AI stories by item set (p. 6, Diversity; p. 8, Figure 8). GPT-4 theme summaries in Table 5 are descriptive labels, not additional theme-count outcomes.

contrasts.reported: Human stories are described as having significantly more themes than model stories. Figure 8 plots the theme counts; numerical counts, an exact p-value and a test statistic are not printed.

diversity_detail.metric: Number of theme clusters from agglomerative clustering with Ward variance minimization; threshold 0.6.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Not explicitly named in the theme-clustering paragraph (p. 6); gte-large is named for story embeddings in the semantic-diversity method (p. 4).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Embeddings of all stories for a given item set; Figure 8 reports separate human and AI theme counts. The clustering paragraph does not explicitly say that the two creator groups are clustered separately.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Not stated. The text says significantly more themes but gives no p-value, interval or test method for the theme-count comparison.
diversity_detail.notes: Set-level outcome; the number of analytic sets is not explicitly stated, so n_units is null. The corpus size is not used as a set count.

outcomes.name: Novelty (Karampiperis et al. 2014 semantic-distance novelty of dominant terms)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Semantic-distance novelty of dominant terms (lemmatized content words), relative to the reference corpus, normalized to [0, 2] (p. 4, Novelty). Methods describe the reference as all stories across item sets; the Limitations section instead describes human and AI stories for each item set (p. 9). The cue-word-distance stratification is a variant (p. 6; p. 22, Figure 14a).

contrasts.reported: "human stories are more novel than those of the models with varying levels of significance across item sets (p < 0.01, p < 0.1, p < 0.05 and p < 0.05)"; Figure 3 (figure only).

outcomes.name: Surprise (mean semantic distance between consecutive sentences)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean semantic-distance change between consecutive story sentences, normalized to [0, 2] (p. 4, Surprise). The sentence-position surprise profiles and low/high cue-word-distance stratification are variants (pp. 6-7, Figure 7; p. 22, Figure 14b).

contrasts.reported: "We see that human stories are more surprising (p < 0.001) than those of the models." Figure 4 (figure only).

outcomes.name: Lexical complexity (story length in unique words)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of unique words in a story (p. 5, Complexity and Figure 5). The low/high cue-word-distance stratification is a variant (p. 7, Complexity; p. 20, Figure 11a). Other lexical-complexity measures are named in notes.

contrasts.reported: AI stories have a larger number of unique words (p < 0.001, reported jointly with longer dependency paths). Figure 5 supplies graphical distributions; numerical arm means and SDs are not printed.

outcomes.name: Syntactic complexity (average dependency path length)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Average length of dependency paths for each word in a sentence (p. 5, Complexity). The low/high cue-word-distance stratification is a variant (p. 7, Complexity; p. 20, Figure 11b). Other syntactic-complexity measures are named in notes.

contrasts.reported: AI stories have longer dependency paths per sentence (p < 0.001, reported jointly with a larger number of unique words). Figure 6 supplies graphical distributions; numerical arm means and SDs are not printed.

eligibility.reason: The study compares independently generated stories from 60 LLMs with unassisted human stories; it does not randomly assign people to AI assistance (p. 3, Story Generation Data Collection). The retained writer sample is 59 people, exceeding the 50-person threshold (p. 3). Creativity and related dimensions are scored on the stories by automated metrics and judges (pp. 4-5, Story Evaluation; p. 8, Table 2). It therefore remains AI-versus-human context evidence and is not eligible for the core dataset. The independent judges are not additional writers.

one_line_finding: Human stories scored higher than stories from 60 LLMs on semantic and lexical diversity (p < 0.0001, p. 5), surprise (p < 0.001, p. 6), and expert-rated creativity (3.58 vs 2.33 on a 5-point scale, t = −19.34, Table 2, p. 8), while non-experts (2.45 vs 3.65, t = 12.76) and LLM judges (2.41 vs 4.26) rated the AI stories as more creative (Table 2, p. 8; p. 7).
notes: The entire markdown conversion and all PDF pages, including references and appendices, were read. The form limit is 15 structured outcomes. Overall creativity ratings are listed first because the paper focuses further judge analyses on creativity (p. 7); primary remains not_stated because no outcome is explicitly designated primary. Existing outcome IDs are preserved despite the new order. The selected outcomes retain the main automated dimensions, all three overall-creativity judge types, all expert component ratings, non-expert originality/effectiveness, and separate lexical and syntactic complexity measures. Omitted as separate structured outcomes due to the limit: non-expert surprise and LLM originality, surprise and effectiveness ratings (p. 8, Table 2). Their printed descriptive results are: Table 2, Non-expert Judges, surprise: Human 2.21 (±0.81) vs AI 2.96 (±0.78); parentheses report SDs. The subset contains 273 stories; creator-specific story counts are not stated. Table 2, LLM Judges, originality: Human 2.33 (±0.73) vs AI 4.22 (±0.72); parentheses report SDs. Human n = 208 stories; AI n = 223 stories (p. 23, Table 10). Table 2, LLM Judges, surprise: Human 2.01 (±0.79) vs AI 3.74 (±0.77); parentheses report SDs. Human n = 208 stories; AI n = 223 stories (p. 23, Table 10). Table 2, LLM Judges, effectiveness: Human 2.86 (±0.58) vs AI 4.14 (±0.52); parentheses report SDs. Human n = 208 stories; AI n = 223 stories (p. 23, Table 10). Also omitted as separate structured outcomes: average word length in characters, Flesch reading ease, average sentence length in unique words, and average constituency tree depth (p. 19, Figure 10); average noun, adjective, pronoun and adverb ratios (p. 18, Figure 9); and first-person, second-person, third-person singular and third-person plural pronoun use (p. 21, Figure 12). The repeated n-gram frequencies in Table 1 (p. 6) are descriptive lexical-repetition diagnostics and are not extracted as separate outcomes. Surprise profiles by sentence position and cue-word-distance stratifications are variants of retained outcomes, described in measure_detail (p. 7, Figure 7; p. 20, Figure 11; p. 22, Figures 13-14). Turing-test creator-classification accuracy, rater reliability/correlations, and the regression predicting ratings from automated scores are not creativity/diversity contrasts and are not extracted as additional outcomes (pp. 5, 7-8, Table 3). Non-expert originality and effectiveness have statistics_available=[none] because the allowed categories do not include means/SDs without arm-specific ns or inferential statistics; the printed means and SDs are retained in reported. For all outcomes, mixed denotes a corpus combining model-generated and unassisted human-generated stories; question=none and comparison_type=ai_vs_human do not imply human AI assistance. The lexical-diversity plot uses a corpus-level axis label while the methods define a story-level ratio; this ambiguity is retained in S1-O7 rather than treated as a confirmed across-writer homogenization measure.
